A good low-key family option when larger parks are fully booked. The lake is warm and shallow — ideal for young children. Very easy to get to from the Snohomish–Monroe corridor. Typically has availability even on summer weekends.

Name: Kayak Point Regional Park
Short Description: Snohomish County park on Puget Sound with 30 water & electric sites (35 ft max) overlooking Saratoga Passage. Great for beach walking, kayaking, and wildlife viewing close to Seattle.
Reservation window: Reserving 6 months in advance
Long description: Kayak Point Regional Park occupies a rare stretch of undeveloped Puget Sound shoreline in Snohomish County, with 3,000 feet of beach frontage and sweeping water views across Saratoga Passage toward Whidbey Island and the Olympic Mountains. The 30 water-and-electric sites accommodate RVs up to 35 feet in a forest of mature firs above the beach — most sites have at least partial water views. The park's 700-foot fishing pier is one of the longest public fishing piers on Puget Sound, popular for perch, small salmon, and crabbing. A boat launch serves kayakers and small powerboats. Great blue herons nest in the old-growth forest, and bald eagles are commonly sighted hunting the shoreline. The beach at low tide reveals clams, oysters, and rich tidal life.

Things to do for families summary: 700-foot Puget Sound fishing pier, beach and tidal exploration, kayaking, and exceptional bird watching from a forested shoreline overlooking the Olympic Mountains.
Nearby nature & parks: Kayak Point Regional Park protects a forested headland above Port Susan Bay, where the protected bay is one of the most important wintering grounds for waterfowl and Pacific Flyway shorebird staging areas in the greater Puget Sound. Port Susan Bay has been designated a marine preserve, recognizing its exceptional eelgrass beds, Dungeness crab nursery habitat, and significance as wintering habitat for canvasback, greater scaup, and surf scoter arriving from across interior Canada. The campground's elevated position above the bay provides panoramic views of the Olympic Mountains across the water, and the park's forest trails descend through mature second-growth to one of the cleanest remaining saltwater beaches on the eastern Puget Sound shoreline.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Sites near the 700-foot pier (1–15) are best — bring crab rings and fish from the dock for Dungeness crab, perch, and salmon. Stunning Puget Sound views with the Cascades visible on clear days. Small park that fills on summer weekends. The rocky beach at low tide is excellent for exploring. Good for kayakers — launch directly from the beach below camp.

Name: Wenberg County Park
Short Description: Snohomish County park on Lake Goodwin with 70 sites including full-hookup options (45 ft max). Popular warm-water lake for water skiing and fishing near Stanwood.
Reservation window: Reserving 6 months in advance
Long description: Wenberg County Park sits on the north shore of Lake Goodwin, a 625-acre warm-water lake known for water skiing, wakeboarding, and bass fishing in Snohomish County. The 70-site campground is organized into loops with a mix of full-hookup sites, partial-hookup sites, and standard sites — accommodating RVs up to 45 feet. A boat launch, swim beach, and playground make it a well-rounded family destination. Lake Goodwin is one of the few lakes near the Puget Sound metro area warm enough for comfortable summer swimming. Nearby Camano Island State Park adds hiking options. The park is located near Stanwood, with good grocery and fuel access, and a Costco in Marysville less than 25 miles away.

Kayaking
Things to do for families summary: Warm-water lake near Stanwood with water skiing, boating, swimming, and bass fishing — one of the closest full-hookup county campgrounds to the greater Seattle area.
Nearby nature & parks: Wenberg County Park sits on Lake Goodwin in the Snohomish County lowlands, a small glacial lake whose relatively undeveloped shoreline maintains riparian habitat for nesting osprey, kingfisher, and great blue heron in a rapidly urbanizing corridor. Lake Goodwin supports populations of rainbow trout, largemouth bass, and yellow perch, and the park's protected waterfront provides one of the few remaining public lake access points in a shoreline increasingly dominated by private development. The surrounding Snohomish River lowlands connect to the Ebey Slough and Snohomish River estuary, important Chinook salmon rearing areas and one of the most significant remaining river delta ecosystems on the eastern Puget Sound shore.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Lake Goodwin waterfront sites (1–30) fill first — the lake has the warmest swimming water in the area. Hookup sites in the back loops. A great family option when Camano Island parks are full. The lake warms quickly in early summer. Easy access from I-5 makes this a convenient overnight. The boat launch is handy for canoe and kayak access.

Name: Silver Lake Park
Short Description: Whatcom County lake campground near Maple Falls with two water-and-electric RV areas, seasonal showers, paddling, fishing, and forest trails.
Reservation window: Reservations for the next calendar year open the first business day of December
Long description: Silver Lake Park is a 410-acre Whatcom County park in the Cascade foothills, about 40 minutes east of Bellingham. Maple Creek and Red Mountain are the park's two RV campgrounds, both with water and electric hookups; a separate Cedar campground is intended for tents, cars, and vans, and a reservable group camp also accepts RVs. The lake has a boat launch and seasonal canoe, kayak, rowboat, pedal boat, and paddleboard rentals. Campground connector, forest canopy, and equestrian trails add options away from the water.
Address: 9006 Silver Lake Rd, Maple Falls, WA 98266
Things to do for families:
Fishing for rainbow and coastal cutthroat trout
Boating with a 10-horsepower motor limit
Seasonal canoe, kayak, and paddleboard rentals
Swimming and lakeside picnics
Campground Connector and Canopy Loop trails
Black Mountain equestrian trail
Playground
Things to do for families summary: Lake fishing, small-boat paddling, forest trails, and a playground in the Cascade foothills east of Bellingham.
Nearby nature & parks: Silver Lake Park covers 410 acres in Whatcom County's Cascade foothills near Maple Falls. Its 5.75-mile trail system connects the lake, three campground areas, quiet forest canopy, meadows, and the base of Red Mountain. Silver Lake is a local fishing and boating destination for rainbow and coastal cutthroat trout, with a 10-horsepower motor limit that keeps the water oriented toward smaller craft.
Amenities summary: Vault toilets are available in each campground. Maple Creek and Red Mountain add seasonal flush toilets and showers; drinking water and a seasonal dump station are available.
Site Recommendations: Choose Maple Creek for the easiest access to the boat launch, beach, picnic area, and playground. Red Mountain sits about three-quarters of a mile from the lake and suits campers who prefer woods, meadow edges, hiking, or equestrian access. Cedar Campground does not allow vehicles over 25 feet and is not recommended for RVs. Whatcom County reports no cell service or Wi-Fi, so save maps and reservation details before arrival.
Access note: Maple Creek and Red Mountain accept RVs; Cedar is not recommended for RVs and prohibits vehicles over 25 feet.

Name: Pine Village KOA Holiday
Short Description: Full-service KOA on the Wenatchee River near Leavenworth with 105 sites (60 full hookup + 45 water & electric, 60 ft max). Walk to Leavenworth's Bavarian village from your campsite.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Pine Village KOA Holiday occupies a prime stretch of the Wenatchee River just 3 miles from Leavenworth's famous Bavarian-themed village. The 105-site campground offers 60 full-hookup sites and 45 water-and-electric sites accommodating RVs up to 60 feet, all in a ponderosa pine forest above the river. KOA's signature amenities include a heated pool, playground, camp store, propane fill, and seasonal activities programming. Tubing the Wenatchee River is a beloved summer activity — tube rentals are available near the park. Leavenworth offers excellent restaurants, festivals (Oktoberfest, Christmas Lighting), and is the gateway to dozens of Icicle Creek and Enchantments hiking trails. Wenatchee's Costco is 25 miles away, and the Wenatchee Valley's fruit orchards and wineries make excellent day trips.
Things to do for families:
Tubing (Wenatchee River)
Hiking (Icicle Creek, Enchantments)
Leavenworth Bavarian village
Swimming pool
Fishing
Biking
Wine country touring
Festivals (Oktoberfest, Christmas Lighting)
Things to do for families summary: Riverside KOA steps from Leavenworth's Bavarian village with river tubing, heated pool, Enchantments hiking access, and year-round festivals.
Nearby nature & parks: Pine Village KOA sits near Leavenworth in the Icicle Creek drainage, at the convergence of the Cascade Mountain front and the broad Wenatchee River valley — a landscape where 8,000-foot granite peaks rise directly above an apple-orchard valley floor in one of Washington's most dramatic topographic transitions. The Icicle Creek corridor above Leavenworth provides trail access to the Alpine Lakes Wilderness and the Enchantments, while the Tumwater Canyon downstream on US-2 offers Class IV whitewater alongside bighorn sheep visible on the canyon walls. The Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest surrounding the Leavenworth basin encompasses a diverse east-Cascades ecosystem where species from the maritime west slope and the arid Columbia Plateau meet in the Wenatchee River watershed.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Pull-through hookup sites are most convenient for larger rigs. Sites near the stream in the back of the property are the quietest and most scenic. The pool and playground make this an excellent family choice. Summer shuttle service to Leavenworth's Bavarian village runs on weekends — very convenient. Book well in advance for July and August; this fills completely. Premium amenities justify the higher nightly rate.

Name: Thousand Trails Leavenworth
Short Description: Large membership RV resort on the Wenatchee River with 225 seasonal sites near Leavenworth. Membership or associate pass required — extensive amenities on 300 acres of ponderosa pine forest.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Thousand Trails Leavenworth is a sprawling membership-based resort on the Wenatchee River offering 225 seasonal sites across 300 forested acres of ponderosa pine. Note: access requires a Thousand Trails membership or a NACO/partner associate pass — casual walk-up camping is not available. For members, the amenities are exceptional: multiple pools, tennis courts, a rec hall, activities staff, fishing on the Wenatchee River, and easy access to Leavenworth and Icicle Creek trails. Sites accommodate various RV sizes; the forested setting means some sites have limited length due to trees. Open seasonally (approximately April through October). Non-members should consider Pine Village KOA (3 miles away) as a comparable alternative with full public reservations.
Things to do for families:
Swimming (multiple pools)
Fishing (Wenatchee River)
Hiking (Icicle Creek, Enchantments)
Tennis
Leavenworth Bavarian village
Activities programming
Biking
River access
Things to do for families summary: Membership resort on the Wenatchee River with multiple pools, activities programming, and access to Leavenworth's Bavarian village and Icicle Creek trails. Membership required.
Nearby nature & parks: Thousand Trails Leavenworth sits in the Icicle Creek valley surrounded by the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, with proximity to the Alpine Lakes Wilderness and one of Washington's premier steelhead and cutthroat trout fisheries in the Icicle River below camp. The Stuart Range's granite towers visible from the valley are the centerpiece of the largest expanse of exposed granite in the Cascades — a batholith surfaced through millions of years of erosion and now hosting some of the finest alpine climbing in North America. The Leavenworth area's east-slope ponderosa pine forest and shrub-steppe transition zones support a distinctive bird community including white-headed woodpecker, flammulated owl, and Lewis's woodpecker at the western edge of their Rocky Mountain range.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Sites near Icicle Creek (1–40) are the most scenic and most in demand. Paved sites throughout make manoeuvring easy for large RVs. Walking distance to Leavenworth's Bavarian-themed downtown — a unique and genuinely fun experience. Membership required; day passes sometimes available for one-time guests. The creek-side sites with mountain views are among the best private RV sites in the Cascades.

Name: Tall Chief RV Park & Campground
Short Description: Popular private RV park on the Snoqualmie River in Fall City with 180 sites (water & electric, 45 ft max). Only 30 minutes from Seattle — the closest RV-friendly private campground to the city.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Tall Chief RV Park occupies a flat stretch of the Snoqualmie River in Fall City, making it one of the most conveniently located private campgrounds for Seattle-area residents — just 25 miles from downtown. The 180 water-and-electric sites accommodate RVs up to 45 feet on level gravel pads, with mature cottonwoods and alder providing shade along the river. The Snoqualmie River is popular for tubing and rafting, and famous Snoqualmie Falls (268 feet, tallest in Washington) is just 6 miles away. Issaquah's retail corridor — including a Costco — is 10 miles west. The park is a popular overflow option when Cascade-area campgrounds are full, and its easy I-90 access makes it a convenient first or last night stop for mountain camping trips.
Address: 35 E Branch Rd SE, Fall City, WA 98024
Things to do for families:
Snoqualmie Falls (6 mi)
River tubing
Fishing
Hiking (Snoqualmie Valley Trail)
Cycling
North Bend shopping & dining
Casino (Snoqualmie Casino, 4 mi)
Things to do for families summary: The closest private RV campground to Seattle — riverside setting near Snoqualmie Falls, 30 minutes from the city with Issaquah Costco 10 miles away.
Nearby nature & parks: Tall Chief RV Park sits in the Snoqualmie Valley near Carnation, where the Snoqualmie River flows through one of the most productive agricultural valleys in Washington in a broad lowland flanked by the Cascade Mountain front to the east and the Issaquah Alps to the west. The Snoqualmie River through this valley stretch is critical coho and Chinook salmon habitat, and bald eagles concentrate here during chum salmon runs each December — sometimes reaching 50+ birds along a single river reach. Tiger Mountain State Forest, the Cascade foothills trail systems, and the Rattlesnake Mountain Scenic Area give this valley one of the most accessible natural recreation environments within 30 miles of downtown Seattle.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Snoqualmie River sites (1–20) are the most scenic. Full hookup sites throughout. Peaceful evening atmosphere once day campers leave. Good for exploring Snoqualmie Falls (7 miles) and the Snoqualmie Valley rail trail. Often has last-minute availability on weekdays. A pleasant, well-maintained private park that punches above its weight.

Name: Packwood RV Park & Campground
Short Description: Full-hookup private RV park in the mountain town of Packwood with 87 sites (40 ft max). Perfect base camp for Mount Rainier's south entrance, White Pass skiing, and Gifford Pinchot National Forest.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Packwood RV Park sits in the heart of Packwood, a small mountain community on US-12 at the junction of several major outdoor recreation corridors. The 87 full-hookup sites (30-amp) accommodate RVs up to 40 feet, with the town's restaurants, general store, and bakery all walkable. Mount Rainier's Ohanapecosh entrance is just 12 miles north, providing access to the stunning Grove of the Patriarchs old-growth trail and Paradise without the crowded northwest-side traffic. White Pass Ski Area is 20 miles east on US-12. The Cowlitz River runs behind town for fishing and wildlife viewing. Iron Creek Campground (Gifford Pinchot NF) and Walupt Lake are accessible day trips. This is arguably the best private RV base camp for Mount Rainier south-side exploration.
Things to do for families:
Mount Rainier National Park (Ohanapecosh, 12 mi)
White Pass skiing (20 mi)
Fishing (Cowlitz River)
Hiking (Gifford Pinchot NF)
Wildlife viewing
Walupt Lake
Things to do for families summary: Best private base camp for Mt. Rainier's south side — 12 miles to Ohanapecosh and the Grove of the Patriarchs, with White Pass skiing 20 miles east.
Nearby nature & parks: Packwood sits in the upper Cowlitz River valley at the intersection of three major wilderness areas — Mount Rainier National Park to the north, the Goat Rocks Wilderness to the northeast, and the William O. Douglas Wilderness to the east — one of the most wilderness-proximate RV towns in Washington. The Cowlitz River through Packwood carries glacial sediment year-round from Mount Rainier's active glacial system, and the river supports wild steelhead and salmon runs managed jointly by state and tribal fisheries authorities in this volcanic watershed. White Pass Ski Area just east of town offers summer hiking access to Pacific Crest Trail ridges, while the Goat Rocks Wilderness PCT traverse to the northeast is widely considered one of the most scenic high-route passages on the entire 2,650-mile trail.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Tree-lined sites (1–30) are the most private. Pull-through sites available for big rigs. Walking distance to Packwood's handful of excellent restaurants (especially for elk burgers). The best RV base for Mt Rainier's Ohanapecosh entrance and Goat Rocks Wilderness trailheads. Often has availability when the national park campgrounds are fully booked — a practical alternative.

Name: American Heritage Campground
Short Description: Full-hookup private campground near Olympia with pool, mini-golf, and forested sites. Easy I-5 access with Costco 10 minutes away — ideal for families heading to or from the Oregon Coast.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: American Heritage Campground is a full-amenity private campground on the south side of Olympia, offering the convenience of I-5 proximity with the feel of a genuine forested retreat. Sites are shaded by mature second-growth fir and cedar, with full hookups accommodating large rigs. The on-site swimming pool, mini golf, playground, and camp store make it a popular family destination. Olympia's state capitol, Percival Landing waterfront, and the hands-on children's museum are less than 10 miles away. Millersylvania State Park is just 8 miles south for hiking and lake activities. The campground is strategically located for Oregon Coast-bound travelers, sitting right at the I-5/US-101 interchange. Olympia's Costco is about 10 miles north.
Things to do for families:
Heated outdoor swimming pool (summer)
Mini golf
Vintage playground
Animal viewing farm (chickens, ducks, sheep)
Paved bicycle riding track
Horseshoe pits
Dog park
Grassy playfield
Olympia State Capitol (8 mi)
Millersylvania State Park (8 mi)
Percival Landing waterfront
Olympia Farmers Market
Things to do for families summary: Family-friendly forested campground near Olympia with pool and mini golf — easy I-5 access for coast-bound travelers, Costco 10 miles away.
Nearby nature & parks: American Heritage Campground sits near Olympia within easy reach of the Nisqually National Wildlife Refuge — one of the most productive river delta ecosystems in the Pacific Northwest, where the Nisqually River draining Mount Rainier's glaciers meets Puget Sound in an internationally significant marsh. The Nisqually Delta hosts wintering flocks of dunlin numbering in the tens of thousands, along with concentrations of northern pintail, green-winged teal, and great blue herons — and the refuge boardwalk is one of the most accessible world-class birding sites in Washington. Millersylvania State Park and Capitol Forest are nearby, providing access to old-growth forest and 80+ miles of multi-use trails in the South Puget Sound's most significant remaining natural landscape.
Amenities summary: Full-service amenities include flush toilets, tiled showers, laundry room, and on-site drinking water. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator. On-site camp store stocked with firewood, propane, RV supplies, ice, and snacks. Unique on-site extras: paved bicycle riding track, animal viewing farm (chickens, ducks, and sheep), horseshoe pits, grassy playfield, dog park, and vintage playground. Heated outdoor swimming pool open in summer. Open year-round.
Site Recommendations: Full hookup pull-through sites are the main draw for self-contained RV travellers. The heated pool and clubhouse make this feel more like a resort than a campground. Well-maintained and convenient for I-5 corridor travellers heading to or from Olympia. A comfortable overnight or base camp rather than a destination. The Tumwater Historical Park and Millersylvania State Park are both within 10 miles.

Name: Andersen's Oceanside RV Park
Short Description: Oceanfront private RV park on the Long Beach Peninsula with 60 full-hookup sites, 50/30/20-amp service, and direct beach access.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Andersen's Oceanside RV Park has 60 full-hookup RV sites on a seven-acre property on the Long Beach Peninsula. The operator lists 50/30/20-amp power, water, sewer, and a picnic table at every RV site, plus a sandy path to the beach. Downtown Long Beach is 3.5 miles away, Ocean Park is 6 miles away, and Cape Disappointment and Ilwaco are about 9 miles away. Reservations are required and same-day arrivals must book before noon.
Things to do for families:
Beach walking (28-mile ocean beach)
Razor clam digging

Fishing (charter boats, Ilwaco)
Whale watching
Long Beach boardwalk
Cape Disappointment State Park (8 mi)
Things to do for families summary: Oceanfront sites on the 28-mile Long Beach Peninsula with razor clamming, kite flying, storm watching, and Cape Disappointment State Park just 8 miles south.
Nearby nature & parks: The park sits on the Pacific side of the Long Beach Peninsula with direct access to the peninsula's broad sandy shoreline. The operator places downtown Long Beach 3.5 miles away, Ocean Park 6 miles away, and Ilwaco and Cape Disappointment about 9 miles away, making the campground a practical base for beach walks and peninsula day trips.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. No fire pits are provided.
Site Recommendations: The operator groups its 60 sites into premium, forest, and prime areas. Ask about the premium end sites for the widest pads and closest beach access; the forest sites are seasonal and may have limited satellite reception. Reservations are required, and same-day arrivals must book before noon.

Short Description: Year-round private RV park across from Birch Bay with full hookups and walkable access to the bay, restaurants, and local activities.

Long description: Beachside RV Park is a year-round private campground across Birch Bay Drive from the protected waters of Birch Bay. The local destination organization lists 72 sites and describes the park as ten minutes from Canada and twenty minutes from Bellingham. Full-hookup RV sites, a walkable waterfront setting, and nearby restaurants make it a practical northern Washington stop; confirm current site dimensions and availability directly with the operator.

Beachcombing

Kayaking

Nearby nature & parks: Birch Bay's broad, shallow saltwater shoreline warms at low tide and supports easy beach walks, paddling, bird watching, and seasonal shellfish exploration. Birch Bay State Park is a short drive south, adding more public shoreline, forest, and picnic space, while the Canadian border and Bellingham are straightforward day trips from camp.

Save the campground phone number before arrival because the operator website currently has a certificate problem.

Name: Sunnyside RV Park
Short Description: Full-hookup private RV park in the Yakima Valley wine country with 35 sites (65 ft max, 50 amp). Yakima Valley's longest-pull-through private park, minutes from dozens of wineries.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: Sunnyside RV Park is one of the most RV-spacious private campgrounds in eastern Washington, with 35 full-hookup, 50-amp sites accommodating rigs up to an impressive 65 feet — ideal for large fifth wheels and Class A motorhomes with tow cars. The park sits in the heart of the Yakima Valley at Sunnyside, surrounded by the wine grape vineyards, hop fields, and apple orchards that make this valley Washington's agricultural engine. Over 200 wineries operate within 30 miles, and the Sunnyside area hosts the annual Sunnyside Hot Air Balloon Stampede each August. Yakima is 25 miles west for Costco and major retail. Kennewick/Richland/Pasco (Tri-Cities) is 45 miles east. The saltwater pool is a popular summer amenity. This is the premier private park for wine country touring in the Yakima Valley.
Things to do for families:
Wine country touring (200+ wineries)
Hop field tours
Fruit stand shopping
Saltwater pool
Hot Air Balloon Stampede (August)
Yakima Valley cycling
Off-road vehicle areas nearby
Things to do for families summary: Prime Yakima Valley wine country base with 65 ft pull-throughs, saltwater pool, and access to 200+ wineries, hop fields, and the annual Hot Air Balloon Stampede.
Nearby nature & parks: Sunnyside sits in the lower Yakima Valley in the heart of Washington's largest wine-producing region, where the Columbia Plateau's basalt landscape creates a sun-baked, semi-arid environment receiving just 8 inches of rain annually in the rain shadow of the Cascades. The Yakima River corridor supports populations of mink, river otter, and great blue heron in the cottonwood gallery forest threading through otherwise agricultural terrain, and the river remains a managed wild steelhead fishery despite decades of agricultural water use. The Yakima Canyon scenic highway 20 miles north provides access to some of the finest raptor-watching terrain in the Columbia Basin, with nesting golden eagles and prairie falcons on the canyon walls above one of Washington's most productive blue-ribbon trout streams.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, showers, and drinking water are all on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Full hookup pull-through sites available for big rigs. Clean, well-maintained, and practical — a comfortable base for Yakima Valley wine country touring and apple orchard visits. Close to grocery stores and Yakima's restaurants. More of a practical overnight stop than a destination, but very comfortable and good value. The Yakima Valley wine trail extends in both directions from here.

Name: Denny Creek Campground
Short Description: Shaded National Forest campground along South Fork Snoqualmie River with easy access to Franklin Falls and Denny Creek Trail, 46 minutes from Seattle.
Reservation window: Reserving 6 months in advance
Long description: Denny Creek Campground sits under a shaded forest canopy along the South Fork Snoqualmie River, offering immediate access to creekside water play and several trails including Franklin Falls and Denny Creek Trail that lead into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The 24 sites accommodate RVs up to 36 feet on paved pads with electric hookups. Easy highway access off I-90 Exit 47 makes this one of the closest National Forest campgrounds to Seattle.
Things to do for families:
Franklin Falls Trail (easy, 2-mile round trip to waterfall)
Denny Creek Trail water slides and swimming holes
South Fork Snoqualmie River wading
Picnicking along the creek
Alpine Lakes Wilderness day hikes
Wildlife watching (deer, black bear, birds)
Things to do for families summary: Creekside camping near Franklin Falls and Denny Creek water slides, just off I-90.
Nearby nature & parks: Denny Creek sits in the heart of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest within the I-90 corridor, at the gateway to the Alpine Lakes Wilderness — one of Washington's most heavily visited wilderness areas, featuring over 700 lakes and tarns scattered across a glaciated landscape. The South Fork Snoqualmie River above the campground carves through ancient rock sculpted by multiple glaciations, and the Denny Creek water slides — a series of smooth granite chutes worn by the river — are among the most popular natural water features in the Cascades. Snoqualmie Pass, visible on the ridge above camp, is one of only five year-round crossings of the Washington Cascades and marks the dividing line between the wet, forested west slopes and the drier rain-shadow forest of the east side.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets and drinking water are available, but no showers on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Sites near Denny Creek (1–12) are the nicest and closest to the famous Keekwulee Falls trail — one of the most popular family hikes in the Cascades. This campground fills every summer weekend; book as soon as reservations open. A great family campground for a first Cascades camping experience. Snowshoe Falls and Lake Melakwa are both reachable on day hikes from camp.

Name: Salmon La Sac Campground
Short Description: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest campground between the Cle Elum and Cooper Rivers with 67 sites; one published pull-through accepts equipment up to 127 feet.
Reservation window: Check Recreation.gov for currently available dates
Long description: Salmon La Sac Campground has 67 sites for tents and RVs between the Cle Elum and Cooper Rivers; Recreation.gov currently lists 40 as reservable. The campground provides drinking water, trash collection, vault toilets, picnic tables, and campfire rings. Site 20 is a 127-foot pull-through, but many sites are much shorter, so match the booking to your full equipment length.
Address: Salmon La Sac Rd, Cle Elum, WA 98922
Things to do for families:
Cle Elum River swimming and wading
Fishing for trout on the Cooper River
Waptus Lake trail (day hike or backpack)
Alpine Lakes Wilderness access
Wildlife watching (elk, deer, osprey)
Scenic drives along Salmon La Sac Road
Things to do for families summary: Riverfront camping at a major Alpine Lakes Wilderness trailhead, great for fishing and swimming.
Nearby nature & parks: Salmon La Sac sits at the upper end of the Cle Elum River valley in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the threshold of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness where the forest gives way to rock and ice above 5,000 feet. The Cooper River and Cle Elum River confluence near camp is a historic salmon spawning reach where coho and Chinook once ran in abundance — and hatchery supplementation programs are actively working to restore wild fish runs to this upper watershed. The Waptus Lake trail from Salmon La Sac leads into the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, a 393,000-acre protected landscape that contains more glacially-carved lakes than any comparable area in the Cascades, including the legendary Enchantments above Leavenworth.

Excellent base for Ingalls Lake, Enchantments day hikes, and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness from the eastern approach. Typically less crowded than the I-90 corridor campgrounds on non-holiday weekends. Good trout fishing in the Cle Elum River directly from camp.

Name: Bumping Lake Campground
Short Description: Two-section National Forest campground on Bumping Lake in the Naches Ranger District with 61 sites and access to excellent trout fishing.
Reservation window: Reserving 6 months in advance
Long description: Bumping Lake Campground sits at 3,400 feet elevation along the shores of Bumping Lake in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. The campground has two sections: the upper section (30 ft max) offers lakefront sites among the pines, while the lower section (50 ft max) has more spacious pull-throughs. Both sections share access to excellent trout fishing on the reservoir, a boat launch, and trails into the William O. Douglas Wilderness. Vault toilets and potable water are available.
Things to do for families:
Trout fishing on Bumping Lake reservoir
Boating and kayaking (boat launch on site)
William O. Douglas Wilderness hiking
Swimming in the lake
Wildlife watching (deer, black bear, eagles)
Scenic photography of Cascade peaks
Things to do for families summary: High-elevation lake camping with great trout fishing and Wilderness trail access in the Naches district.
Nearby nature & parks: Bumping Lake sits in a high valley of the Wenatchee National Forest, surrounded by old-growth forest at the edge of the William O. Douglas Wilderness — a 167,000-acre roadless area named for the Supreme Court Justice who was a passionate Pacific Northwest hiker. The Douglas Wilderness protects an intact Cascade mountain ecosystem from the Cascade Crest down to the Naches River drainage, encompassing volcanic meadows, alpine lakes, and old-growth forest largely unaltered since Douglas first explored it in the 1940s. Bumping Lake's position below the Cascade Crest places it in the transition zone between the wetter maritime climate of the west slope and the drier continental climate of eastern Washington, creating a mosaic of forest types and exceptional biodiversity.
Amenities summary: Vault toilets and drinking water are available, but no showers on site. Fire pits are listed as available; check current fire restrictions with the operator.
Site Recommendations: Sites near Bumping Lake (1–20) fill first for the water access and mountain views. The lake is good for motorized boating and fishing — rare on NF campgrounds. Can be windy in the afternoon; sheltered sites mid-loop are better for tent camping. A more remote feel than I-90 campgrounds. Good base for William O. Douglas Wilderness day hikes and the American Ridge trail system.
Coordinates source: https://www.recreation.gov/api/camps/campgrounds/232356
Coordinate precision: official facility point; confirm entrance routing

Name: La Wis Wis Campground
Short Description: One of Gifford Pinchot's largest campgrounds with 122 sites off Highway 12 near Packwood at the confluence of the Cowlitz and Ohanapecosh Rivers.
Reservation window: Reserving 6 months in advance
Long description: La Wis Wis is the largest campground in Gifford Pinchot National Forest, with 122 sites spread across a beautiful river terrace where the Cowlitz and Ohanapecosh Rivers meet. RV sites accommodate rigs up to 40 feet. The campground's Highway 12 location makes it ideal for exploring both Mount Rainier National Park (25 miles north) and the Packwood/White Pass area. Flush toilets, drinking water, and a camp host are on site. The adjacent rivers offer fishing and wading, and the grove of old-growth Douglas fir provides exceptional shade.

Cowlitz and Ohanapecosh River fishing and wading
Day trips to Mount Rainier National Park (25 mi)
White Pass ski area and hiking trails nearby
Ohanapecosh hot springs (in Rainier NP)

Old-growth Douglas fir grove walks

Nearby nature & parks: La Wis Wis sits at the confluence of the Cowlitz and Ohanapecosh Rivers in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest, within the vast volcanic landscape shaped by Mount Rainier and the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens visible 25 miles to the southwest. The Ohanapecosh River above the campground flows from hot springs within Mount Rainier National Park and through the Grove of the Patriarchs — one of the oldest old-growth forests in the Cascades — before reaching camp in a rush of crystal-clear glacial melt. White Pass and the Goat Rocks Wilderness just to the east protect the most rugged remaining volcanic landscape between Rainier and Adams, with the Pacific Crest Trail traversing alpine ridges offering panoramic views of all three southern Washington volcanoes.

The Lewis River watershed drains the southern flanks of Mount St. Helens and the northern approaches to Mount Adams, and the river corridor supports wild steelhead and coho salmon runs that still draw tribal and sport fishermen to the canyon's deep pools. Short Description: Gifford Pinchot National Forest campground near Trout Lake with 30 sites in a scenic meadow-edge setting, popular for berry picking and Bigfoot Country exploration.

Long description: Peterson Prairie Campground sits at 2,900 feet near Trout Lake in the southern Gifford Pinchot National Forest, in an area famously called "Bigfoot Country" by locals. The 30 sites accommodate RVs up to 32 feet in a forested meadow-edge setting. Huckleberry picking in late summer is legendary here, and the area offers hiking to nearby lava tubes and the Indian Heaven Wilderness. Vault toilets and potable water are on site.

Huckleberry picking (late August–September)
Ice Cave lava tube exploration

Things to do for families summary: Meadow-edge campground near Trout Lake with legendary huckleberry picking and lava tube caves.
Nearby nature & parks: Peterson Prairie sits in a high meadow of the Gifford Pinchot National Forest with commanding views of Mount Adams — Washington's second-highest peak at 12,281 feet — and access to the Indian Heaven Wilderness, a high-altitude plateau studded with over 150 huckleberry-ringed lakes. The Indian Heaven area is one of the most significant traditional gathering sites for tribal nations of the Columbia Plateau, who gathered annually to harvest huckleberries that still grow in extraordinary abundance across the volcanic meadows. Ice Cave, just 3 miles from camp, is a lava tube where year-round ice persists in the upper chambers — a remnant of a volcanic eruption that created an underground cave system insulated from summer heat by the thick basalt walls.

Loop B has pull-through sites for equestrian campers. The meadow setting is beautiful and the huckleberry fields in late summer are exceptional. Book early when the Ice Caves are open. Bring warm layers — the high elevation meadow is cooler than the Columbia River corridor below.

The Baker Lake watershed above the campground includes Cascade River tributaries that flow through some of the most productive Pacific salmon habitat in the North Cascades — and the restoration of salmon passage above Upper Baker Dam is one of Washington's most significant in-progress fisheries recovery projects. Mount Baker's intense volcanic heat produces the highest snowfall ever recorded at a US weather station — 95 feet in one winter — and the resulting glacial meltwater draining into Baker Lake is what gives the lake its distinctive aquamarine tint visible from the campground.

Name: Bogachiel State Park
Short Description: RV campground on the Bogachiel River near Forks in the heart of Olympic Peninsula rainforest. Six water/electric hookup sites and a dump station; Hoh Rainforest is 20 miles east.
Reservation window: Reservable up to 9 months in advance
Long description:
Bogachiel State Park sits on the banks of its namesake river — one of the wild salmon waterways draining out of Olympic National Park — in the old-growth rainforest corridor south of Forks. The 123-acre park is blanketed in Sitka spruce and western red cedar, the kind of forest where the canopy closes overhead and the light turns green. It's a quiet, under-visited campground that mostly serves people who know the Olympic Peninsula well.

Six west-loop sites have water and electric hookups (up to 40 feet). The remaining west-loop sites are hookup-free standard sites that accommodate RVs and are positioned along the river — the east loop (sites 30–42) is tent-only. Highway 101 runs along the eastern edge of the campground, and log trucks hauling timber out of the Hoh Valley use it around the clock. Request a west-facing river site if noise is a concern; the river provides good sound cover on that side.

Forks is 6 miles north with a full grocery store, fuel, and basic supplies. Hoh Rainforest — one of only a few temperate rainforests in the United States — is about 20 miles east on Upper Hoh Road. The Hall of Mosses trail is 45 minutes of walking and one of the most distinctive landscapes in the Pacific Northwest. Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort is 30 miles northeast; Ruby Beach and the Pacific coastline are 30 miles south on US-101.
Things to do for families:
Bogachiel River fishing for salmon and steelhead
Hoh Rainforest day trip — Hall of Mosses trail (45 min walk)
Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort (30 miles northeast)
Ruby Beach and Pacific Coast tide pools (30 miles south)
Forks town exploration — Twilight tourism, local diners
Things to do for families summary: Fishing the Bogachiel River, day-tripping to the Hoh Rainforest, and easy access to Olympic National Park's most iconic destinations. The nearby town of Forks is the Olympic Peninsula's main hub for resupply and Twilight tourism.
Nearby nature & parks: Olympic National Park begins just miles from the campground — the Bogachiel River Trail heads directly into the park's wilderness from a trailhead 3 miles north. Hoh Rainforest is 20 miles east via Upper Hoh Road, and Sol Duc Valley is 30 miles northeast on US-101. Ruby Beach on the Pacific Coast is 30 miles south.
Amenities summary: Flush toilets, coin-operated showers, drinking water, and fire pits listed as available. Dump station on site. The six hookup sites (water and electric) are in the west loop.

For non-hookup RV sites in the west loop (sites 7–29), request the river-facing side: the Bogachiel River is audible and the old-growth canopy is at its thickest here. Avoid the US-101-adjacent sites on the east side of the loop — log trucks run that highway through the night. The east loop (sites 30–42) is tent-only.

Name: Elwha Dam RV Park

Full hookups with 30/50 amp service, fiber optic Wi-Fi, hot showers, laundry, and a clubhouse make this a comfortable home base for extended stays. The Sol Duc Hot Springs, Rialto Beach, and Hoh Rainforest are all reachable as day trips. Elwha River access from the park means real fishing for returning salmon and steelhead — a direct result of the dam removal and one of conservation's great comeback stories.

The park stays open year-round and winter stays are quieter with easier site availability.

Name: Whidbey Island Fairgrounds Campground
Short Description: The only public campground on South Whidbey Island — 20 RV sites with power and water hookups, a 15-minute walk to downtown Langley's galleries and waterfront, and South Whidbey State Park's old-growth forest eight miles north.
Reservation window: Reserving 3 months in advance
Long description: The Fairgrounds Campground at Port of South Whidbey is the only public RV campground on the island's southern half — a useful basecamp for exploring the art galleries, whale watching, and old-growth forests of South Whidbey. The 20 RV sites sit on the fairgrounds property in Langley, with power and water hookups (50/30/20 amp; no sewer). A public dump station is on-site for $5. Bathrooms with private showers are available. The campground is a 15-minute walk from downtown Langley, a compact arts community with restaurants, galleries, the South Whidbey Historical Museum, a whale museum, and the Seawall Park overlook above Saratoga Passage. South Whidbey State Park, preserving 53 acres of old-growth Douglas-fir and beachfront on Admiralty Inlet, is 8 miles north. The Clinton ferry terminal to Mukilteo is 6 miles south, making mainland day trips straightforward. Reservations available via RoverPass, or claim an empty site on arrival. Limited water hookups November–March. Maximum 14-night stay.
Time from Seattle: ~1 hr 30 min from Seattle (via Mukilteo–Clinton ferry)
Things to do for families:
Stroll to downtown Langley's galleries, whale museum, restaurants, and waterfront overlook (15-min walk)
Langley Seawall Park whale-watching platform above Saratoga Passage
South Whidbey State Park old-growth forest trails and Admiralty Inlet beach (8 miles north)
Double Bluff Beach — expansive off-leash dog beach with Olympic Peninsula views (6 miles northwest)
Kayaking and paddleboarding on Saratoga Passage from nearby launches
Clinton–Mukilteo ferry for mainland day trips (6 miles south)
Fort Casey Historical State Park lighthouse and underground gun batteries (30 min north)
Freeland Park freshwater lake swimming and picnicking (10 miles north)
Things to do for families summary: The only public campground on South Whidbey, 15 minutes on foot from Langley's art galleries and whale-watching waterfront, with South Whidbey State Park old-growth forest and Saratoga Passage close by.
Nearby nature & parks: South Whidbey State Park preserves 53 acres of old-growth Douglas-fir and offers beach access on Admiralty Inlet, 8 miles north on Hwy 525. Double Bluff Beach, an expansive off-leash dog beach with sweeping views of the Olympic Mountains, is 6 miles northwest. Langley's Seawall Park sits at the base of the bluff below downtown with a whale-watching platform over Saratoga Passage. Fort Casey Historical State Park with lighthouse and underground batteries is 30 minutes north.
Amenities summary: 20 RV sites with power and water hookups (50/30/20 amp, no sewer). On-site public dump station ($5 fee). Bathrooms with private showers. Reservations via RoverPass or walk-in. Open year-round with limited water hookups November–March.
Site Recommendations: Reserve ahead via RoverPass for summer visits — the 20-site campground fills quickly on weekends when Langley festivals draw crowds. Premium 50-amp sites are worth the few extra dollars if running high-draw appliances. Walk-in sites are sometimes available for spontaneous arrivals. The campground can get noisy during the Whidbey Island Fair (typically August) — check the fairgrounds calendar if quiet nights are a priority. Winter stays offer solitude and easy availability.

Name: Dosewallips State Park
Short Description: Hood Canal state park with standard, water-and-electric, and full-hookup camping for RVs up to 40 feet, plus river and shoreline access.
Reservation window: Reservable up to 9 months in advance
Long description: Dosewallips State Park spans both sides of Highway 101 where the Dosewallips River reaches Hood Canal. The developed campground mixes standard sites with water-and-electric and full-hookup options, and the park accommodates RVs and vehicle-trailer combinations up to 40 feet. Campers have access to flush restrooms, showers, drinking water, a dump station, forest trails, river access, and a Hood Canal shoreline. Camping is offered year-round, though water service is limited to a smaller winter loop from mid-November through March.
Things to do for families:
Walk the forest and river trails
Explore the Hood Canal shoreline
Fish the Dosewallips River and Hood Canal
Swim or paddle when conditions allow
Watch for elk, eagles, and marine wildlife
Things to do for families summary: A flexible Hood Canal base for river walks, shoreline exploring, fishing, and paddling.
Nearby nature & parks: The park connects a lowland forest and the Dosewallips River with Hood Canal shoreline, making it easy to experience several Olympic Peninsula habitats in one stop. Olympic National Park trailheads lie farther up the Dosewallips valley, while nearby Seal Rock adds another public shoreline and a short interpretive trail.
Amenities summary: Flush restrooms, showers, drinking water, and a dump station serve the developed campground. Water service is reduced in winter.
Site Recommendations: Use the current campground map to match your rig and hookup needs: sites 2–5 and 11–40 are marked full hookup; sites 53–58, 71–73, and 77–92 are marked water and electric. From November 15 through March 31, the park says water is available only at sites 21–29. Individual pad length varies, so confirm your exact equipment length while booking.
Access note: Official park guidance allows RVs and vehicle-trailer combinations up to 40 feet; individual site limits vary.

Name: Fort Flagler Historical State Park
Short Description: Spacious RV camping on Marrowstone Island with standard, partial, and full-hookup sites, beaches, historic batteries, and rigs up to 50 feet.
Reservation window: Reservable up to 9 months in advance
Long description: Fort Flagler Historical State Park occupies the north end of Marrowstone Island, with broad views across Admiralty Inlet and Port Townsend Bay. Its two developed campgrounds offer different experiences: the Lower Campground has standard, partial-hookup, and full-hookup sites near the water, while the Upper Campground has more private standard sites in the forest. Official park materials list 59 standard and 55 full-hookup sites and accommodate RVs up to 50 feet. Campers can walk historic coastal-defense batteries, hike shoreline trails, paddle from the beach, and use flush restrooms, showers, drinking water, and a dump station.
Things to do for families:
Explore historic gun batteries and military buildings
Walk beaches and shoreline trails
Kayak or paddleboard on protected water
Fish and watch boats in Admiralty Inlet
Visit the park museum and interpretive displays
Things to do for families summary: Historic fort exploration, beach walks, paddling, and roomy campground loops on Marrowstone Island.
Nearby nature & parks: Fort Flagler sits where Port Townsend Bay meets Admiralty Inlet, with shoreline on three sides and long views toward Whidbey Island and the Olympic Mountains. The park's trails link beaches, bluff overlooks, forest, and the remains of the Harbor Defenses of Puget Sound. Fort Worden and Fort Casey form the other two points of the historic Triangle of Fire and make natural follow-on stops.
Amenities summary: Flush restrooms, showers, drinking water, and a dump station serve the developed campgrounds.
Site Recommendations: Choose the Lower Campground for water views and standard, partial-hookup, or full-hookup choices; choose the Upper Campground for a quieter forest setting with standard sites. The lower campground is reservable year-round beginning in 2026, while upper-loop availability changes seasonally. Confirm the length limit for the exact site even though the park accommodates RVs up to 50 feet.
Access note: Official park materials list RV accommodation up to 50 feet; individual site limits vary.
